title: Get the Strategic Sequence Right
coreMove: Run a promising idea through utility, price, cost, and adoption in sequence before excitement turns it into a launch.
sourcePressure: Test promising ideas in order: buyer utility, strategic price, target cost, and adoption, so novelty becomes commercially viable value innovation.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Assuming buyer enthusiasm or originality is enough to prove a blue-ocean move is ready.

sourceAnchors.name: buyer utility, price, cost, and adoption sequence
sourceAnchors.detail: official invention-versus-innovation support summarizes the idea-index sequence including adoption
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The sequence is unforgiving: first utility, then price, then cost, then adoption, with each gate able to stop a beautiful idea.

sourceAnchors.name: value innovation
sourceAnchors.detail: official support says value innovation happens only when buyer utility, price, and cost line up
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Value innovation is the point where usefulness, price, and cost stop fighting one another.

hook: Do not open with a competitor scoreboard, a war metaphor, or a generic market map.
Do not use A crowded market is not..., The real strategy is..., or What if growth... as reusable shells.
counterintuition: Avoid Most people assume... but actually... and The opposite is true.
Avoid turning every chapter into competition bad, creativity good.
tryThisNow: Avoid Set a timer for 60 seconds and list... as a repeated action.
Avoid generic reflect on your strategy prompts.
examples: Avoid conference-room whiteboard workshops as the default scene.
Avoid repeating mugs, markers, dosing cups, bike helmets, radiators, bus depots, classrooms, narrow kitchens, or generic dashboard scenes.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: school-safety hardware tested through sequence gates
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder excited by parent reactions at a school fair
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a useful prototype becomes a viable broad-market offer
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she sees that parent praise proves utility but says nothing yet about price, cost, or adoption by schools
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A bright plastic lock prototype sits on a folding table beside a sign-in sheet

exampleSpecs.audience: a local pharmacist serving overwhelmed family caregivers
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether caregivers adopt the service or admire it from a distance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he hears relief from caregivers but must set a price and workflow they will actually accept
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "I would sleep again," a daughter tells Olivier, then asks the monthly price

exampleSpecs.domain: allergy-safe classroom party boxes and target cost
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder balancing parent trust, ingredient cost, and school budgets
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the kit remains safe, affordable, and profitable
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she cuts boutique ingredients to meet target cost without harming the utility parents and teachers need
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Marta one rejected school quote to stop treating premium snacks as sacred

exampleSpecs.domain: digital permit portal adoption by contractors and clerks
exampleSpecs.audience: a public-sector product lead with a promising digital service
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether contractors, clerks, and inspectors use the process or route around it
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he asks about clerks and inspectors before declaring the portal ready, surfacing adoption resistance
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 3:12 p.m., Kiran watches a contractor slide a paper permit under the glass

exampleSpecs.domain: school bus safety route praised before cost reality
exampleSpecs.audience: an operations manager praised for a safer route idea
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a safer route survives driver hours and fuel costs
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he reconstructs how applause for utility hid a broken target-cost structure
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Diesel fumes hang in the yard while Sam adds twelve minutes to each run

exampleSpecs.domain: warehouse VR safety simulator adoption by supervisors
exampleSpecs.audience: a training lead introducing a safety simulator
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the simulator changes practice or sits unused after launch
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she predicts trainee excitement is enough, then supervisors reveal adoption resistance around shift coverage
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Who signs out the headset when the line is already short two people?

skillTargets: order utility, price, cost, and adoption checks
detect when buyer excitement hides a failed later gate
evaluate commercial viability without killing useful novelty too early

tryThisNowSpec: Take one idea you like and write four words in order: utility, price, cost, adoption. Put the weakest gate in a box.
